newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC delegates awaiting impact of Iraqi exports.
newsitem.headline: OPEC delegates awaiting impact of Iraqi exports.

text.p: The prospect of the United Nations easing its Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil exports could halt this year's surprise world oil price rally, industry experts said Tuesday.

While that might bring relief to consumers, the view as OPEC oil ministers gathered for a conference in Vienna was that strong winter demand for fuel meant that the market was not about to collapse anytime soon.
Iraq's U.N. ambassador, Nizar Hamdoon, said Monday that Iraq agreed to conditions that had delayed a pact to let it export oil for the first time since it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
The accord, designed to help Iraq buy food and medicine, had been shelved in September when President Saddam Hussein sent troops to north Iraq to intervene in Kurdish faction fighting.
"The market is hungry for barrels right now," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk for brokers Smith Barney.
That means any decline in prices could be limited and most likely will be delayed until next spring, analysts said.

The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries begins its semi-annual conference on Wednesday, and oil ministers had already figured on a possible resumption of Iraqi exports when they set their production quotas at the last meeting in June.

OPEC's problem is that several of the 11 cartel members are cheating on their mandated quotas, and total OPEC daily volume is already almost a million barrels above the intended ceiling of 25.03 million barrels -- even before Iraqi exports flow.
Violations by members like Venezuela are unlikely to stop, delegates said.

But they added that OPEC was most likely to extend quotas until June 30 and hope for some restraint to prevent too rapid an erosion of prices early next year when peak cold weather fuel demand is over and Iraq may be back.
"It's cold and I hope it gets colder," said OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria.
Cartel president, Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad of the United Arab Emirates, told reporters in Vienna that Iraq would be no problem "on condition each member of OPEC will be restricted to their quota."
Analysts said the effect of Iraq's return to the market will depend on timing and other factors, such as weather.

"The market is tight and it can take anything that is thrown at it right now," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist with UBS Limited in London. "But if Iraq returns soon it could be that prices will soften more quickly in the spring than we had expected."
"It all depends on the timing. If we think the (Iraqi) oil is going to come out in the first quarter of 1997, then it is already factored in and it won't be a big deal," one industry source said.
Hamdoon said in New York on Monday that Iraqi oil could flow as soon as December under the accord to permit sales worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine.
But the deal has repeatedly been held up and sceptical traders noted that technical details including a pricing formula had yet to be finalised.

Energy prices fell on Monday after news of the Iraqi-U.N. accord, but they recovered much of their lost ground Tuesday. Crude oil for January delivery, which fell 26 cents on Monday, added 11 cents to $23.60 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange in early afternoon trading.
